data: Before we choose, can we agree on a shared catch limit? Taking 19 tons each would leave just 5 tons, and a failed replenishment would mean only 10 tons next month. I propose 17 tons each this month: we each earn $17,000, leave 15 tons, and have either 100 or 30 tons next month. Then we adjust our whole-ton quotas to the actual stock, always leaving at least 5 tons. Since everyone’s catch is revealed afterward, we can review whether we kept the agreement. John, would you support that?

Emma, I support a shared limit, but I’d propose 15 tons each as a compromise. Compared with 10 each, that gives every one of us an extra $5,000 this month—$25,000 extra altogether. We’d leave 25 tons, so next month’s stock would be 100 tons with 75% probability or 50 tons with 25% probability. That’s a larger buffer than the 30-ton downside under your 17-ton proposal.

There is a real tradeoff: at 10 each, we leave 50 tons and next month reaches 100 under either recovery outcome. At 15 each, we give up that certainty. If we get the 50-ton outcome, we cannot repeat 15 each; we would need to negotiate lower catches. For example, 5 each would leave 25, yielding either 100 or 50 the following month. That future agreement would be voluntary, not enforced, and revealed catches only let us review compliance afterward.

John, would you commit to 15 this month? Kate and Jack, would you each join us? Emma, would you accept $2,000 less this month than your proposal in exchange for that larger downside buffer? I commit to choosing 15 tons this month myself. Can each of you explicitly say whether you’ll do the same, or name a whole-ton alternative you would accept?

I’ll join Luke in choosing 15 tons this month. That earns us more than the 10-ton plan while keeping a meaningful buffer, provided everyone sticks to the limit.

Let’s also agree now on the downside: if next month starts at 50 tons, we each take 5 tons; if it starts at 100, we each take 15 again. Neither rule guarantees natural replenishment, but both leave 25 tons and avoid having to renegotiate from scratch after a bad draw. If anyone exceeds the agreement, let’s discuss how to repair it rather than retaliating by emptying the lake—that would hurt all of us.

John, will you join the 15-ton agreement and the 5-ton fallback?

I’ll join: 15 tons this month, and 5 tons each if next month’s stock is 50. If all five follow that rule, we leave 25 tons in either case and avoid collapse, even when natural replenishment fails. Let’s keep that standing agreement while everyone complies, and review any unexpected stock level before choosing again. I also agree that a breach should prompt discussion, not destructive retaliation. Kate, are you willing to join? Emma, would you accept this plan instead of 17?

I’m in: 15 tons this month, then 15 each at a stock of 100 or 5 each at 50. I’ll stick to those limits even after a bad replenishment draw; the lower catch is what keeps the agreement viable over time. If we encounter a different stock level, let’s agree on revised whole-ton limits before fishing, keeping at least 5 tons in the lake. Emma, you’re the last to confirm—will you join us?
